newsitem.title: USA: Lutherans reject merger with Epsicopalians.
newsitem.headline: Lutherans reject merger with Epsicopalians.

text.p: - Leaders of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America Monday narrowly rejected an agreement formally recognizing the Episcopal Church, which had approved the move last month.

At the same time, the Lutherans agreed to end doctrinal differences that date back to Martin Luther's time with three other Protestant churches. The pact means each denomination will recognize the clergy and liturgy of the others.

The Evangelical Lutheran's Churchwide Assembly, meeting here, voted 839-193 to approve "full communion" with the Presbyterian Church-USA, with 2.7 million members; the United Church of Christ, with 1.5 million congregants, and the 400,000 members of the Reformed Church in America.
The two-thirds vote for "full communion" came despite some doctrinal and theological differences stressed by opponents within the assembly. These were aired during weekend debate.
The vote to merge with the Episcopal Church fell six votes short of the required two-thirds.

All Protestant churches emphasize an individual's direct relationship with God through the Bible. But the churches differed on the meaning of the Eucharist. These differences remain unresolved, but they were overlooked by the majority of Lutheran delegates.
Slightly more than one third of delegates to the Lutheran's convention could not accept the Episcopalian doctrine called "apostolic succession."

By holding that the clergy derives its authority from Christ's apostles, the Episcopal Church retains the basis of a strong central authority. The opposition believes that the congregation in each church holds authority.
The Episcopal Church has 2.5 million congregants, while the Evangelical Lutherans have 5.2 million. Leaders of the Episcopal Church approved the merger in July.
